'''''Bixa orellana''''', also known as '''achiote''', is a [[shrub]] or small tree native to Mexico and Central and South America.<ref name=IUCN/><ref name="cabi">{{cite web |title=''Bixa orellana'' (annatto) |url=https://www.cabi.org/isc/datasheet/9242 |publisher=Center for Agriculture and Biosciences International (CABI) |access-date=10 October 2018 |date=27 September 2018}}</ref><ref name="morton">{{cite journal |first=Julia F. |last=Morton |title=Can Annatto (''Bixa orellana'', L.), an old source of food color, meet new needs for safe dye? |url=http://journals.fcla.edu/fshs/article/view/101136/97080 |journal=Proceedings of the Florida State Horticultural Society |volume=73 |pages=301–309 |access-date=10 October 2018 |year=1960 |archive-date=11 October 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181011013753/http://journals.fcla.edu/fshs/article/view/101136/97080 }}</ref> ''Bixa orellana'' is grown in many countries worldwide.<ref name=cabi/>

The plant is best known as the source of [[annatto]], a natural orange-red condiment (also called {{lang|es|achiote}} or {{lang|und-Latn|bijol}}) obtained from the waxy [[aril]]s that cover its seeds.<ref name=cabi/><ref name=morton/> The ground seeds are widely used in traditional dishes in [[Central America|Central]] and [[South America]], [[Mexico]], and the [[Caribbean]], such as ''[[cochinita pibil]]'', chicken in {{lang|es|achiote}}, {{lang|es|caldo de olla}}, and {{lang|ppl|[[nacatamal]]}}. Annatto and its extracts are also used as an industrial [[food coloring]] to add yellow or orange color to many products such as [[butter]], [[cheese]], margarine, ice creams, meats, and condiments.<ref name=cabi/> Some of the [[indigenous people of the Americas|indigenous peoples]] of North, Central, and South America originally used the seeds to make red [[body paint]] and [[lipstick]], as well as a spice.<ref name="morton" /> For this reason, the ''Bixa orellana'' is sometimes called the '''lipstick tree'''.<ref name=cabi/><ref name=morton/>

==Etymology and common names==
The name ''Bixa orellana'' was given by [[Carl Linnaeus|Linnaeus]]. The botanical [[genus]] name derives from the aboriginal [[Taíno language|Taíno]] word "bixa", while the [[specific epithet]] was derived in honor of the Amazon explorer [[Francisco de Orellana]], an early explorer of the [[Amazon River]].<ref name=morton/><ref>{{cite book |last1=Levy |first1=Luis W. |last2=Rivadeneira |first2=Diana M. |editor1-last=Lauro |editor1-first=Gabriel J. |editor2-last=Francis |editor2-first=F. Jack |year=2000 |title= Natural Food Colorants Science and Technology |series=IFT Basic Symposium Series |location= New York |publisher=Marcel Dekker |isbn=978-0-8247-0421-6 |page=115 |chapter=Annatto}}</ref> The name ''achiote'' derives from the [[Nahuatl]] word for the shrub, {{lang|nah|āchiotl}} {{IPA|nah|aːˈt͡ʃiot͡ɬ|}}. It may also be referred to as {{lang|und-Latn|aploppas}}, or by its original [[Tupian languages|Tupi]] name {{lang|tup|uruku}}, {{lang|tup|urucu}} or {{lang|tup|urucum}} ("red color"), which is also used for the body paint prepared from its seeds.<ref name=cabi/> Colloquial names include ''bija'', ''roucou'', ''orellana'', ''annatto'', ''achiote'', and many other names used regionally.<ref name=cabi/> The nickname, "lipstick tree", derived from use of the dye as a [[cosmetics|cosmetic]].<ref name=morton/>

==Description==
''Bixa orellana'' is a perennial, tall shrub to small evergreen tree that can reach {{convert|20-33|ft|m|0|abbr=on|order=flip}} high.<ref name=cabi/><ref name=morton/><ref>{{Cite web |url=http://plants.usda.gov/plant-profile?symbol=BIOR |title=Plants profile for ''Bixa orellana'' (lipsticktree) |publisher=Plants database, US Department of Agriculture |access-date=2019-04-19}}</ref> It bears clusters of {{convert|2|in|cm|0|abbr=on|order=flip}} bright white or pink flowers, resembling single wild roses, that appear at the tips of the branches.<ref name=cabi/> The fruits of the ''Bixa orellana'' are globular, ovoid capsules arranged in clusters resembling spiky looking red-brown seed pods covered in soft spines.<ref name=cabi/> Each capsule, or pod, contains 30–45 cone-shaped seeds covered in a thin waxy blood-red [[aril]].<ref name=cabi/> When fully mature, the pod dries, hardens, and splits open, thereby exposing the seeds.<ref name=cabi/>

The plant is most well known as the source of the red-orange annatto pigment. The pigment is derived from the waxy aril layer that covers the seeds of the ''Bixa orellana'' fruit.<ref name=cabi/><ref name=morton/> The red-orange annatto dye is rich in the [[carotenoid]] [[pigment]]s, 80% which consists of [[bixin]] (the red pigment) and [[norbixin]] or orelline (the yellow pigment).<ref name=cabi/><ref name=":0" /><ref name="jar">{{cite journal |last1=Ul-Islam |first1=S. |last2=Rather |first2=L. J. |last3=Mohammad |first3=F. |year=2015 |title=Phytochemistry, biological activities and potential of annatto in natural colorant production for industrial applications – A review |journal=Journal of Advanced Research |volume=7 |issue=3 |pages=499–514 |doi=10.1016/j.jare.2015.11.002 |pmc=4856788 |pmid=27222755}}</ref>
Annatto oil contains [[tocotrienol]]s, [[beta-carotene]], [[essential oil]]s, [[saturated fat|saturated]] and [[unsaturated fat|unsaturated fatty acids]], [[flavonoid]]s, and [[vitamin C]].<ref>{{cite web |last1= Ângela de Almeida Meireles |first1= Maria |first2= Carolina |last2= Lima Cavalcante de Albuquerque |title= Processo otimizado para obtenção de óleo rico em antioxidantes de urucum |work= Inova |publisher= Unicamp |url= http://www.inova.unicamp.br/sici/visoes/ajax/ax_pdf_divulgacao.php?token=QyjKaJjh |format= PDF |access-date= 2 Jun 2015 |language= pt }}</ref>

==Genomics==
A chromosome-scale genome assembly of ''Bixa orellana'' was published in 2026. The assembled genome size is approximately 270 Mb and includes 10 chromosome-scale superscaffolds representing 96.4% of the assembly. The assembly showed a BUSCO completeness of 98.6%, and approximately 56,000 transcripts were annotated. The genome was generated to facilitate studies of genes involved in [[bixin]] biosynthesis and regulation.<ref name="Lieberman2026">{{cite journal

==Distribution==
Although the exact origin of ''Bixa orellana'' is unknown, it is native to northern South America and the Central American tropics: "it is said to be indigenous by Seemann on the northwest coast of Mexico and Panama, by Triana in New Granada, by Meyer in Dutch Guiana, and by Piso and Claussen in Brazil".<ref name=morton/> Additionally, ''Bixa orellana'' is found in substantial wild and cultivated acreages from [[Mexico]] to [[Ecuador]], [[Brazil]], and [[Bolivia]].<ref name=cabi/> Although an [[invasive species]], it is cultivated in many world regions.<ref name=cabi/>

During the 16th and 17th centuries, the annatto dye was distributed to [[Southeast Asia]], Africa, the [[Caribbean]], Hawaii and southeastern North America in tropical and subtropical regions through trading exchanges.<ref name=cabi/><ref name=morton/> It became cultivated in tropical regions of Asia, such as India, Sri Lanka, and Java mainly for the dye which the seeds yield.<ref name=cabi/>

==Cultivation==
[[File:Bixa.jpg|thumb|Achiote flower]]
[[File:Bixa orellana fruit roucou kourou 2.jpg|thumb|right|Mature achiote pods, showing the red seeds]]
''Bixa orellana'' grows easily in subtropical to tropical climates, in frost-free regions sheltered from cool winds.<ref name=cabi/> It prefers year-round moisture, good drainage, and moderately fertile soil in full sun or partial shade. It can be propagated from seed and cuttings. Cutting-grown plants flower at a younger age than seedlings.<ref>Lord, Tony (2003) ''Flora : The Gardener's Bible : More than 20,000 garden plants from around the world''. London: Cassell. {{ISBN|0-304-36435-5}}.</ref>

The main commercial producers of ''B. orellana'' are countries in Latin America (specifically Peru, Brazil and Mexico), which constitute 60% of total world production followed by Africa (27% of total world production) and Asia (12% of total world production).<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Raddatz-Mota |first1=Denise |last2=Pérez-Flores |first2=Laura J. |last3=Carrari |first3=Fernando |last4=Mendoza-Espinoza |first4=José A. |last5=de León-Sánchez |first5=Fernando Díaz |last6=Pinzón-López |first6=Luis L. |last7=Godoy-Hernández |first7=Gregorio |last8=Rivera-Cabrera |first8=Fernando |date=May 2017 |title=Achiote (Bixa orellana L.): a natural source of pigment and vitamin E |journal=Journal of Food Science and Technology |volume=54 |issue=6 |pages=1729–1741 |doi=10.1007/s13197-017-2579-7 |issn=0022-1155 |pmc=5430180 |pmid=28559632 |display-authors=3}}</ref>{{Better source needed|reason=The article does not focus on global cultivation (more about pigment synthesis) and does not cite the source of their production statistics|date=February 2019}} Production statistics are not usually available and would not provide a reliable guide to international trade, since many of the producing countries use significant quantities domestically (e.g., Brazil is a large producer and consumer, needing additional imports). Annual world production of dried annatto seed at the beginning of the 21st century was estimated at 10,000 tons, of which 7,000 tons enter international trade. Peru is the largest exporter of annatto seed, annually about 4,000 tons; Brazil the largest producer, with about 5,000 tons. Kenya exports annually about 1,500 tons annatto seed and extracts and is the second-largest exporter, after Peru. Côte d'Ivoire, Angola, and the Philippines are also exporters.<ref>{{cite web |first= P. C. M. |last= Jansen |editor-last= Jansen |editor-first= P. C. M. |editor2-last= Cardon |editor2-first= D. |title= Bixa orellana L. |work= PROTA 3: Dyes and tannins/Colorants et tanins |publisher= PROTA |date= 2005 |url=http://database.prota.org/PROTAhtml/Bixa%20orellana_En.htm |access-date= 5 Oct 2014 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20081120191458/http://database.prota.org/PROTAhtml/Bixa%20orellana_En.htm |archive-date= 20 November 2008}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1= |first1= |title=Phl exports 'atsuete' to Vietnam|url=https://www.philstar.com/business/agriculture/2013/07/14/965511/phl-exports-atsuete-vietnam |access-date=August 3, 2024 |publisher= [[The Philippine Star]]|date=July 14, 2013}}</ref>

==Industrial uses==
[[File:Urucum virgim oil.JPG|thumb|Oil of ''Bixa orellana'']]
Before synthetic dyes revolutionized industry, ''Bixa orellana'' (which is the only plant to produce the [[pigment]] [[bixin]])<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Bouvier|first1=Florence|last2=Dogbo|first2=Odette|last3=Camara|first3=Bilal|date=2003|title=Biosynthesis of the Food and Cosmetic Plant Pigment Bixin (Annatto)|journal=Science|volume=300|issue=5628|pages=2089–2091|doi=10.1126/science.1085162 |jstor=3834418 |pmid=12829782 |bibcode=2003Sci...300.2089B |s2cid=560600 |issn=0036-8075}}</ref> was planted commercially. The pigment is extracted from the pericarp of the seeds through use of alkaline water, vegetable oil, or organic solvents.<ref name=cabi/><ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last1=Vilar |first1=Daniela de Araújo |last2=Vilar |first2=Marina Suênia de Araujo |last3=Moura |first3=Túlio Flávio Accioly de Lima e |last4=Raffin |first4=Fernanda Nervo |last5=Oliveira |first5=Márcia Rosa de |last6=Franco |first6=Camilo Flamarion de Oliveira |last7=de Athayde-Filho |first7=Petrônio Filgueiras |last8=Diniz |first8=Margareth de Fátima Formiga Melo |last9=Barbosa-Filho |first9=José Maria |display-authors=3 |date=2014 |title=Traditional Uses, Chemical Constituents, and Biological Activities of Bixa orellana L.: A Review |journal=The Scientific World Journal |language=en |volume=2014 |article-number=857292 |doi=10.1155/2014/857292 |issn=2356-6140 |pmc=4094728 |pmid=25050404|doi-access=free }}</ref>

The annatto pigment has global economic significance, as it is one of the most widely used natural dyes to color food, cosmetics and pharmaceutical products. It is used commonly in foods because the coloring does not alter the flavor and is not toxic,<ref name=morton/> though it may trigger allergic reactions in those who are sensitive.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Mikkelsen |first1=H. |last2=Larsen |first2=J. C. |last3=Tarding |first3=F. |chapter=Hypersensitivity Reactions to Food Colours with Special Reference to the Natural Colour Annatto Extract (Butter Colour) |series=Archives of Toxicology |date=1978 |volume=1 |editor-last=Leonard |editor-first=B. J. |title=Toxicological Aspects of Food Safety |chapter-url=https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-642-66896-8_16 |issue=1 |language=en |location=Berlin, Heidelberg |publisher=Springer |pages=141–143 |doi=10.1007/978-3-642-66896-8_16 |pmid=150265 |isbn=978-3-642-66896-8|chapter-url-access=subscription }}</ref> It is mainly used to dye [[ice cream]], meats, dairy products (cheeses, butter and margarine) and [[condiments]].<ref name=cabi/><ref name=morton/> Cosmetic products include lipstick, hair coloring products, nail polish, soaps, lacquers and paints.<ref name=morton/>

==Culinary uses==
Ground ''Bixa orellana'' seeds are often mixed with other seeds or spices to form a paste or powder for culinary uses in [[Latin American]], [[Jamaica]]n, [[Chamorro people|Chamorro]], and [[Philippine cuisine|Filipino]] cuisines. The seeds are heated in [[oil]] or [[lard]] to extract their dye and flavor for use in dishes and processed foods such as [[cheese]], [[butter]], [[soup]], [[gravy]], [[sauce]]s, [[cured meat]]s, and other items. The seeds impart a subtle flavor and aroma and a yellow to reddish-orange color to food.

{{anchor|sazón}}
A condiment called {{lang|es|sazón}} is commonly used in Spanish, Latin American, and Caribbean cuisine for meats and fish. The Spanish word {{lang|es|sazón}} means "season" or "seasoning". {{lang|es|Sazón}} is made with ground ''Bixa orellana'' seeds and packaged into small, disposable foil packets for easy use. Additionally, [[cumin]], coriander seeds, salt, and garlic powder are included in these {{lang|es|sazón}} condiment packets.<ref name=":5">{{Cite web |url=https://www.thespruceeats.com/what-is-achiote-or-annatto-2138265 |title=Achiote: The Spice That Dyes Food Yellow |website=The Spruce Eats |language=en |access-date=2019-04-19 |archive-date=2022-07-29 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220729003008/https://www.thespruceeats.com/what-is-achiote-or-annatto-2138265 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

On Spanish-speaking Caribbean islands, the annatto pigment is also used to make yellow rice and is sometimes added to [[sofrito]].<ref name=":5" /> Additionally, in the [[French Caribbean]], it is added to a fish or pork stew called blaff.<ref name=":5" />

In [[Brazil]], a powder known as {{lang|pt|colorau}} or {{lang|pt|colorífico}} is made from the ground seeds combined with filler seeds like [[maize]]. This powder is similar to and sometimes replaces [[paprika]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.hort.purdue.edu/newcrop/proceedings1990/V1-367.html |title=New Crops from Brazil |publisher= Purdue University |year= 1990 |access-date=24 August 2011}}</ref> In [[Nicaragua]], the most common way achiote is used in their [[Cuisine of Nicaragua|cuisine and dishes]] is in the form of a paste. It is used in many national dishes,<ref>{{cite web |url= https://www.laprensa.com.ni/2017/09/30/espectaculo/2305882-el-achiote-un-colorante-saludable |title= El achiote un colorante saludable |language= es |last= Gonzalez |first= Martha |date= 30 Sep 2017 |publisher= Editorial La Prensa S.A. |access-date= 27 Aug 2021 }}</ref> such as chancho con yuca, [[nacatamal]], and [[fritanga]]. The [[Yucatán (state)|Yucatecan]] condiment called {{lang|es|[[recado rojo]]}}, or "achiote paste", is made from ground ''Bixa orellana'' seeds combined with other spices and is a mainstay in [[Mexico|Mexican]] and [[Belize]]an cuisines.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.los-dos.com/recipes/verarticulo.php?IdArticulo=266 |title=RECIPE: Recado Rojo |website=LOS DOS |access-date=2019-04-19}}</ref>

==Traditional uses==
One major traditional use of the ''Bixa orellana'' plant was for body, face, and hair paint among various tribes and ancient civilizations either for decorative purposes or as [[omen]]s to ward off evil spirits and illnesses.<ref name=morton/><ref name=":3">{{Cite journal |last=Donkin |first=R. A. |date=1974 |title=Bixa Orellana: "The Eternal Shrub" |journal=Anthropos |volume=69 |issue=1/2 |pages=33–56 |issn=0257-9774 |jstor=40458510}}</ref> It has been reported to be used by Brazilian native tribes, the native [[Taíno]]s in Puerto Rico, the [[Tsáchila]] of [[Ecuador]] and different Amazonian tribes.<ref name=morton/><ref name=":3" /><ref name=":4">{{cite web |url=http://aic.stanford.edu/sg/bpg/annual/v16/bp16-05.html |title=Colorants Used During Mexico's Early Colonial Period |year=1997 |publisher=Stanford University |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080320051026/http://aic.stanford.edu/sg/bpg/annual/v16/bp16-05.html |archive-date=March 20, 2008 |url-status=live |access-date=24 August 2011}}</ref> As a result of the [[Spanish conquest of the Aztec Empire|Spanish Conquest]], the ''Bixa orellana'' was introduced to peoples like the [[Aztecs]], [[Inca Empire|Incas]] and [[Mochica language|Mochicas]], who showed evidence of later use.<ref name=":3" /> The Aztecs also apparently used the annatto pigment as red ink for manuscript painting in the 16th century.<ref name=morton/><ref name=":4" />

''Bixa orellana'' is used in [[traditional medicine]].<ref name=morton/><ref name=":0" /> The tree has been used in [[Ayurveda]], the folk medicine practices of [[India]], where different parts of the plant are thought to be useful as therapy.<ref>{{cite book |url=https://www.springer.com/medicine/complementary+%26+alternative+medicine/book/978-0-387-70637-5 |title=Indian Medicinal Plants |last=Khare |first=C. P. |date=2007 |publisher=Springer Science+Business Media, LLC |isbn=978-0-387-70638-2 |location=New York}}</ref>

The plant is valued for its stem fiber to make rope mats and for the adhesive gum.<ref>{{cite book | author = Ellison, Don | date = 1999 | title = Cultivated Plants of the World | location = London |publisher=[[New Holland Publishers]] }} <!--(1st ed.: Brisbane: Flora Publications International, 1995)--></ref><ref>{{cite book | author = Graf, Alfred Byrd | date = 1986 | title = Tropica: color cyclopedia of exotic plants and trees for warm-region horticulture—in cool climate the summer garden or sheltered indoors | edition = 3rd | location = East Rutherford, N.J. | publisher = Roehrs Co. }}</ref><ref>{{cite book | author = Macoboy, Stirling | date=1979 | title =  What Tree is That? | location = Sydney, Australia | edition = 1st | publisher = Ure Smith | isbn = 0-7254-0480-9}}</ref>
